message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | Key Rights | How to Exercise Them | |------|------------|----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after lease ends, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs.
• Request a written itemized statement if you believe deductions are improper. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.).
• Must comply with all building, health, and safety codes. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter).
• If unresolved, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment & Late Fees** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are limited to **$25** or **5%** of the monthly rent, whichever is greater. | • Pay on time; if late, pay the fee promptly. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the lease ends. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot disturb your peaceful use of the property. | • Document disturbances; send a written notice to the landlord. | | **Repair and Deduct / Rent Withhold** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may:
 1. Pay for the repair and deduct from rent (only if the repair is necessary for habitability).
 2. Withhold rent until the issue is fixed (must be done in writing and only for major repairs). | • Keep receipts and send a written notice to the landlord. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of entries; if the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes under the Fair Housing Act. | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• Eviction must go through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove tenants. | • Respond to notices promptly; seek legal counsel if you receive an eviction notice. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent control laws. | • Be aware that rent increases must be disclosed in writing and follow lease terms. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise stated in the lease. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease; contact utility companies if services are disrupted. | | **Insurance** | • Landlord is not required to provide renter’s insurance, but it is highly recommended. | • Obtain renter’s insurance to protect personal property. | #### Practical Steps to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand all clauses, especially those about deposits, repairs, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, photos of damages, and a log of maintenance requests. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Send all notices via email or certified mail so you have proof of delivery. 4. **Know the Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections beyond state law. 5. **Seek Legal Aid** – If you face eviction or disputes, consult a tenant‑rights organization or a lawyer specializing in landlord‑tenant law. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general and not legal advice. Laws can change, and local ordinances may add additional protections. For specific legal questions, consult a licensed attorney or a tenant‑rights organization in Texas.
